questions.q: What four-part format does a package version number follow?
options: YEAR.MONTH.DAY.BUILD
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.BUILD
MAJOR.MINOR.BUILD.PATCH
VERSION.RELEASE.STATUS.BUILD
questions.explain: A package version number follows MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.BUILD — for example, 1.2.0.3 — with MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH set by the developer and BUILD assigned by the Dev Hub.

questions.q: Which segment of the version number does the Dev Hub assign automatically, often written as the literal string NEXT in sfdx-project.json?
options: MAJOR
MINOR
PATCH
BUILD
questions.explain: BUILD is incremented automatically by the Dev Hub every time a new version is created at the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; writing "1.2.0.NEXT" tells the Dev Hub to compute it rather than the developer guessing it.

questions.q: What is versionName, and how does it differ from the version number?
options: It's identical in function to the version number, just formatted differently
It's a free-text, human-readable label (like "Spring Release") with no effect on install logic or version ordering
It replaces the need for a version number entirely
It's automatically generated by the Dev Hub and cannot be customized
questions.explain: versionName is purely a human-readable label for release notes and listings; the numeric version number is what Salesforce and installing orgs actually reason about programmatically.

questions.q: What is an ancestor version used for in managed package versioning?
options: It sets the package's namespace
It declares the specific prior version a new version is meant to upgrade from, so Salesforce can validate the upgrade path
It determines the package's installation key
It controls whether the package is Unlocked or Managed
questions.explain: Ancestry declares which specific prior version a new managed package version directly upgrades from, letting Salesforce validate that the upgrade path won't silently break or lose data due to incompatible schema changes.

questions.q: What does the --code-coverage flag do when running sf package version create, and why does it matter for managed packages specifically?
options: It deletes any existing code coverage data
It calculates and records Apex code coverage for the version, which is required before a managed package version can later be promoted to released
It skips all Apex tests during version creation
It only applies to unlocked packages, never managed ones
questions.explain: --code-coverage calculates and records the version's Apex code coverage, and that coverage data is a prerequisite for later promoting a managed package version to released, as covered in the previous lesson.
